implementation_notes: In Kotlin the relay is an ordinary parameter list: Compose's own guidance is that data flows down the UI tree as parameters, which keeps a composable's dependencies explicit and its preview/test setup trivial, and the same holds for constructor parameters in non-UI code. Keep this default while the value is local to a small part of the tree; the cost appears exactly as elsewhere - intermediates declaring parameters they only forward.
pitfalls: Compose function signatures are positional-agnostic only by name; renaming the relayed parameter per level makes the chain untraceable even though the compiler still checks types.
Passing a whole screen-state object down keeps every composable coupled to a type it does not use - prefer narrow parameter types or CompositionLocal.

Keep this default while the value is local to a small part of the tree; the cost appears exactly as elsewhere - intermediates declaring parameters they only forward.

variants.name: CompositionLocal for widely used values
variants.implementation_notes: Compose's scoped-consumption mechanism: `compositionLocalOf` creates a key with a default, `CompositionLocalProvider(LocalX provides value)` binds it for a subtree, and any composable reads `LocalX.current` without the value appearing in intermediate parameters. The Android documentation frames this as the answer to data that is 'very frequently and widely used' (theme, typography, density) and warns against overuse because it makes dependencies implicit.
pitfalls: `staticCompositionLocalOf` does not track reads: changing a static local recomposes the whole subtree below the provider, so it is only for values that never change during composition.
A `LocalX.current` read is invisible in the composable's signature, so previews and tests must remember to provide the value - a missing provider silently returns the default.

variants.name: CoroutineContext elements for coroutine-scoped data
variants.implementation_notes: In coroutine code, ambient per-coroutine data rides in the `CoroutineContext` - an indexed set of elements (since Kotlin 1.3) that is inherited by child coroutines - so a value can be attached once at launch and read with `coroutineContext[MyKey]` at any suspension point instead of being threaded through every suspend function. Use it for genuinely coroutine-scoped values (trace id, tenant, request metadata) and keep business dependencies explicit; elements must be immutable because the context is shared with children.
pitfalls: A context element is immutable and shared with child coroutines: putting mutable state into one element breaks the contract and races between children.
Adding and removing elements creates new context instances; code that holds an old context reference keeps seeing the old value.
